title: AWS Direct Connect Pricing: Costs and Fees in 2026
summary: AWS Direct Connect pricing varies by port speed, location, and data transfer volume. Get specific port fees, regional transfer rates, and sample bills.
body_markdown:
## Monitoring Direct Connect spend with Activepieces


### What the workflow can and can't do


Activepieces can watch a Direct Connect bill on a schedule, and its Free plan, with 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows, covers that check, but it can't lower the bill.


The workflow reads cost from AWS Cost Explorer, compares it with a limit you choose, and tells someone when the circuit costs more than you planned. The saving comes from the audit you do first.


### Auditing all Direct Connect circuit costs first


Start that audit by listing every line that belongs to the circuit, not just the AWS invoice. Port-hours and data transfer out appear on the bill.


The cross-connect fee from the colocation facility and the carrier circuit arrive on separate invoices, and the second connection you bought for redundancy shows up twice in each.


Write down which invoice carries each line and who approves it. Any line with no owner is the one that will surprise you, and AWS can't see it for you.


### Routing Direct Connect cost alerts to team channels


The obvious tool is AWS Budgets, and it covers the basic version of what follows. It can alert on a cost threshold with no extra tooling.


Choose Activepieces when you want the alert to land in a channel your team already reads, or to log each month beside the non-AWS lines that Budgets can't see.


Its published pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run however many steps it has, where Zapier's pricing page bills per task and Make's bills per module, and the Free plan includes 1,000 credits a month with unlimited flows, so a monthly check with a router and a sheet insert costs one credit a run.


Below, a screenshot shows a ten-step flow in the Activepieces builder, titled "Test Flow".


It has a schedule trigger, a Google Sheets step, a loop, a date helper, an HTTP request, two AI steps, a Sheets insert, a router with a "Branch 1" and an "Otherwise" path, and a Gmail send-email step.


It is a different job from ours, but the shape is the one you need: a trigger, a fetch, a decision, then an action. Your version is shorter, and the router is the step that matters.


### Stage 1: pull Direct Connect cost from the AWS bill


Set a schedule trigger to run monthly, or weekly if you want early warning. Add an HTTP request step that calls the Cost Explorer API, using credentials for a user permitted only to read cost data.


Filter the query to the Direct Connect service and group by usage type. Grouping matters because it separates port-hours from data transfer out, so you can see which one moved when the total does. A single total tells you that spend rose, not why.


Next, add a router. Branch 1 fires when the returned cost exceeds your limit; "Otherwise" handles the normal case.


Base the limit on the whole-circuit estimate from your audit, not on last month's AWS figure alone. A limit taken from the AWS invoice only will pass an overrun in any cost that sits on another invoice.


### Sending Direct Connect alerts and logging monthly costs


On Branch 1, send an email or chat message naming the usage type that drove the overage.


On both branches, insert a row in a spreadsheet with the month, the AWS figure, and the carrier and cross-connect amounts you type in by hand.


After a few months that sheet is the whole-circuit cost, built from real invoices and ready to check against the original estimate.
